positions/congregational-polity/oneLine: Each gathered congregation of believers is self-governing under Christ, choosing its own officers, with no binding authority above it.
positions/congregational-polity/coreClai: The local church, a covenanted community of believers, is the full expression of the Church.
Christ rules the congregation directly through his Word; the members together discern his will.
The congregation calls and dismisses its pastors/elders and deacons and exercises discipline (Matt 18:17).
Associations and conventions are voluntary fellowships with advisory, not binding, authority.
positions/congregational-polity/origin: English Separatists such as Robert Browne (A Treatise of Reformation without Tarrying for Any, 1582) and Henry Barrow argued for gathered churches independent of bishops and state. The "Independents" at the Westminster Assembly, the Cambridge Platform of New England (1648) and the Savoy Declaration (1658) formalised it; Baptists, many Pentecostals and most independent evangelical and house churches practise it.
positions/congregational-polity/stronges: It takes seriously the priesthood of all believers and the congregation’s role in discipline and choosing leaders in the New Testament (Matt 18:17; Acts 6:3).
It protects churches from coercion by hierarchies and states, a key factor in the history of religious liberty.
It allows rapid church planting and adaptation, as in Baptist, Pentecostal and house-church expansion.
Episcopal and presbyterian critics argue that it lacks accountability and fosters fragmentation and doctrinal drift.
The New Testament shows apostolic and conciliar authority over multiple churches (Acts 15; the Pastorals).
Congregational votes can marginalise minorities or empower charismatic individuals without checks.
positions/congregational-polity/response: Congregationalists reply that apostolic authority now resides in Scripture, not successors, and that voluntary associations can provide accountability.
They point to the vitality of free churches, e.g. Baptists and house churches, as evidence of its effectiveness.
positions/congregational-polity/conseque: Contributed to the rise of religious liberty and disestablishment, notably in England and America.
Shapes Baptist life worldwide (Southern Baptist Convention, Baptist World Alliance).
Ideal for underground churches under persecution, e.g. Chinese house churches.
positions/womens-ordination-affirmed/one: Women may be called and ordained to all offices of ministry, including pastor, priest and bishop, because in Christ there is "neither male nor female" and the Spirit gifts women for leadership.
positions/womens-ordination-affirmed/cor: Gender is not a barrier to any ministry: the Spirit is poured out on sons and daughters alike (Joel 2:28; Acts 2:17–18).
Women exercised leadership in the New Testament: Phoebe as deacon (Rom 16:1), Junia "of note among the apostles" (Rom 16:7), Priscilla as teacher (Acts 18:26), women prophets (1 Cor 11:5).
Restrictive texts (1 Cor 14:34–35; 1 Tim 2:11–15) addressed specific local situations, not universal rules.
Male-only priesthood rests on cultural assumptions rather than the gospel.
positions/womens-ordination-affirmed/ori: Women deacons existed in the early Church, especially in the East (Council of Chalcedon canon 15), and abbesses exercised authority. Quakers recognised women preachers from the 1650s (Margaret Fell, Women’s Speaking Justified, 1666). Antoinette Brown was ordained by a Congregational church in 1853; Holiness and Salvation Army women (Catherine Booth, Phoebe Palmer) and early Pentecostals (Aimee Semple McPherson) preached widely. Florence Li Tim-Oi became the first Anglican woman priest in 1944; US Methodists granted full clergy rights in 1956; the Church of England ordained women priests from 1994 and bishops from 2014.
positions/womens-ordination-affirmed/pro: N. T. Wright (on Romans 16 and 1 Timothy 2)
positions/womens-ordination-affirmed/str: The new creation in Christ overcomes the hierarchy of the fall (Gal 3:28; Gen 3:16), and Pentecost explicitly includes women prophets.
Romans 16 names women in prominent ministry roles, including one apostle (Junia).
The fruit of women’s ministry in missions, revivals and pastorates is evident across history.
Paul’s restrictions appear tied to particular problems (e.g. false teaching at Ephesus), and other cultural instructions (head coverings, slavery) are not applied literally today.
Catholics and Orthodox argue Christ freely chose only men as apostles and the Church has never ordained women priests, so it lacks authority to do so.
Complementarians argue 1 Timothy 2:12–14 grounds its restriction in creation order (Adam formed first), not culture.
Critics argue women’s ordination has accompanied wider liberal theological shifts in some denominations.
It has caused splits and impaired communion (e.g. Anglican Communion, Old Catholic–Polish National Catholic break in 2003).
positions/womens-ordination-affirmed/res: Egalitarians reply that Jesus’ choice of twelve Jewish men symbolised Israel’s twelve tribes, not a permanent rule (he also chose no Gentiles).
They argue the creation-order reference illustrates deception in the Ephesian context, and that "authority" (authentein) in 1 Timothy 2:12 is a rare word possibly meaning "domineer".
Many evangelical egalitarians hold high views of Scripture, showing the issue is exegetical, not a liberal-conservative divide.
positions/womens-ordination-affirmed/con: Most mainline Protestant and many Pentecostal churches ordain women; by the 2020s women formed a large share of clergy in several Western denominations.
Created tensions in ecumenical relations with Rome and Orthodoxy.
Contributed to divisions within Anglicanism, Lutheranism and Baptists.
positions/womens-ordination-restricted/o: The ordained priesthood (Catholic and Orthodox) or the pastoral/elder office (complementarian Protestants) is reserved to men, though women serve in many other ministries.
positions/womens-ordination-restricted/c: Christ freely chose only men as the Twelve, and the apostles did the same; the Church is bound by this example.
For Catholics and Orthodox, the priest acts in persona Christi, as icon of Christ the Bridegroom, so the sacramental sign requires a male.
For complementarians, men and women are equal in dignity but have distinct, complementary roles grounded in creation (1 Tim 2:12–13; 1 Cor 11:3).
Women’s ministries (deaconess, abbess, teacher of women, missionary, prophet) are honoured and needed.
positions/womens-ordination-restricted/o: The constant practice of Catholic, Orthodox and Oriental churches, formally articulated in response to Protestant ordinations: Paul VI’s Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, Inter Insigniores (1976); John Paul II, Ordinatio Sacerdotalis (1994). Evangelical complementarianism was formalised by the Council on Biblical Manhood and Womanhood’s Danvers Statement (1987); the Southern Baptist Convention’s Baptist Faith and Message (2000) limits the pastoral office to men.
positions/womens-ordination-restricted/s: It has the unbroken support of the Church’s practice across East and West for nearly two thousand years.
Paul grounds his restriction in creation, not in local culture (1 Tim 2:13; 1 Cor 11:8–9).
Jesus defied cultural norms in his treatment of women, so his choice of male apostles was not merely cultural.
Sacramental iconicity: the priest represents Christ the Bridegroom to the Church his bride.
Egalitarians argue it is inconsistent with Galatians 3:28, Pentecost and Paul’s commendation of women leaders (Rom 16).
Historians note that women deacons were ordained by laying on of hands in the early and Byzantine Church, complicating claims of uniform tradition.
Critics argue it can sustain wider patterns of exclusion or abuse of power.
positions/womens-ordination-restricted/r: Catholics and Orthodox reply that the diaconate is distinct from the priesthood and that the question of deaconesses does not affect priestly ordination (Pope Francis’ commissions on women deacons, 2016 and 2020, left this open).
Complementarians stress equality of dignity and broad scope for women’s ministry, and condemn abuse as contrary to servant headship (Eph 5:25).
positions/womens-ordination-restricted/c: The practice of the majority of the world’s Christians (Catholic and Orthodox), as well as many evangelical bodies.
A major obstacle to full communion between Rome/Orthodoxy and Anglicans/Lutherans.
Fuels ongoing debates over women deacons and the scope of women’s leadership in Catholic and evangelical churches.
positions/donatism/oneLine: The Church must be a pure community of the holy; clergy who betrayed the faith in persecution lose the power to administer valid sacraments, so their baptisms and ordinations are void.
positions/donatism/coreClaims/0: The Church is the spotless bride of Christ, a community of the pure separated from the world.
positions/donatism/coreClaims/1: Bishops who were traditores (who handed over Scriptures in the Diocletian persecution) or in communion with them cannot give the Spirit.
positions/donatism/coreClaims/2: Sacraments administered by unworthy or schismatic clergy are invalid, so converts must be (re)baptised.
positions/donatism/coreClaims/3: The true Church is the persecuted Church of the martyrs, not the one allied with the emperor.
positions/donatism/keyTexts/2: Psalm 141:5 (Latin: "let not the oil of the sinner anoint my head")
positions/donatism/keyTexts/3: Cyprian, On the Unity of the Church; Letters on rebaptism
positions/donatism/origin: After the Diocletian persecution (303–305), Caecilian was consecrated bishop of Carthage (c.311) by Felix of Aptunga, accused of being a traditor. Numidian bishops elected Majorinus, then Donatus (from 313). Constantine’s inquiries (Rome 313; Council of Arles 314) found for Caecilian. Drawing on Cyprian’s ecclesiology, the Donatists became the majority church in much of North Africa for a century, with radical Circumcellion bands. Tyconius was a dissenting Donatist theologian.
positions/donatism/strongestArguments/0: It takes holiness and costly faithfulness under persecution with utmost seriousness; restoring betrayers casually dishonours the martyrs.
positions/donatism/strongestArguments/1: It could claim the authority of Cyprian, the great African martyr-bishop, who had rebaptised schismatics.
positions/donatism/strongestArguments/2: It resisted the emerging alliance of Church and empire and the use of state coercion in religion.
positions/donatism/strongestObjections/0: Augustine argued that sacraments belong to Christ, not to the minister: "this is He that baptizeth" (Tractates on John 6.7); otherwise no believer could be sure of their baptism.
positions/donatism/strongestObjections/1: Jesus’ parables of wheat and tares and the dragnet (Matt 13) teach that the visible Church is mixed until the judgement.
positions/donatism/strongestObjections/2: Donatism confined the Church to Africa, contradicting its catholicity throughout the world.
positions/donatism/strongestObjections/3: The Circumcellions’ violence undermined claims to purity.
positions/donatism/responses/0: Donatists replied that a "catholic" church spread worldwide but corrupt was no Church, and that Catholics themselves used imperial violence against them.
positions/donatism/responses/1: Modern historians (Frend) see Donatism also as an expression of North African regional and social identity, which explains its endurance.
positions/donatism/consequences/0: Led to Augustine’s doctrines of sacramental validity and the mixed Church, foundational for Western theology.
positions/donatism/consequences/1: Prompted the first major use of imperial coercion against fellow Christians, which Augustine justified ("compel them to come in", Luke 14:23), a precedent later used to justify persecution.
positions/donatism/consequences/2: Weakened North African Christianity before the Vandal (429) and Arab conquests; Donatist communities persisted into the 7th century.
positions/donatism/consequences/3: "Donatist" became a byword for perfectionist separatism, applied to later movements (Anabaptists, some revivalists).
